subject: General Information
question: What type of state does the 1987 Philippine Constitution declare the Philippines to be?

choices.text: Federal and parliamentary state
Unitary and monarchical state
Socialist and democratic state
Theocratic and republican state
Democratic and republican state

explanation: Article II, Section 1 of the 1987 Constitution — the very first substantive provision after the Preamble — declares: 'The Philippines is a democratic and republican State. Sovereignty resides in the people and all government authority emanates from them.' This twin characterization is foundational: 'democratic' signals rule by the people; 'republican' means government is run through elected representatives accountable to the people, not by a monarch or dictator. Every other provision of the Constitution flows from this single sentence.

distractorExplanations.A: The Philippines has a unitary, not federal, structure, and a presidential, not parliamentary, system. Under a parliamentary system the executive is drawn from the legislature — the Philippine Constitution explicitly separates those branches.
distractorExplanations.B: The Philippines is indeed unitary (not federal), but it is republican — not monarchical. There is no king or queen; the head of state is an elected President.
distractorExplanations.C: Socialism was never adopted as the state character. The Constitution protects private enterprise and acknowledges the role of the private sector (Art. XII, Sec. 20). 'Democratic' appears in the correct answer but paired with 'republican,' not 'socialist.'
distractorExplanations.D: Confusing 'theocracy' (government by religious law) with 'democracy'; Art. II Sec. 1 declares the Philippines a democratic and republican state, not a theocratic one — separation of Church and State is explicit in the Constitution.

tip.label: Constitution Reminder
tip.text: Article II, Sec. 1 = 'democratic and republican.' Think DR — like a Doctor Runs the republic. Every CSE review starts here.

subject: General Information
question: Under the 1987 Constitution, what is the term of office of the President of the Philippines?

choices.text: Five years, not eligible for re-election
Six years, not eligible for re-election
Four years, eligible for one re-election
Six years, eligible for one re-election
Six years, eligible for re-election after sitting out one term

explanation: Article VII, Section 4 is unequivocal: the President serves a single six-year term and is 'not eligible for any reelection.' This ironclad rule was a direct reaction to Ferdinand Marcos, who exploited martial law to extend his presidency beyond two terms. The 1987 Constitution's framers wanted to ensure that no future president could entrench themselves in power. The Vice-President, by contrast, may serve two consecutive terms and is eligible to serve as President after the prohibited period.

distractorExplanations.A: Five years is the term of local officials such as the President under the 1935 Constitution. The 1987 Constitution fixed the presidential term at six years, not five.
distractorExplanations.C: Four years with one re-election is the American presidential model. The Philippines deliberately chose a single longer term with no re-election to prevent the abuses of the Marcos era.
distractorExplanations.D: Six years is correct, but the 'eligible for one re-election' part is wrong. The Constitution explicitly bars any re-election for the President — it is an absolute, not a one-time, prohibition.
distractorExplanations.E: Conflating the presidential term with the vice-presidential re-election rule; Art. VII Sec. 4 imposes an absolute ban on re-election for the President, not just a one-term cooling-off period.

tip.label: Mnemonic
tip.text: President = 6 years, NO re-election. Vice-President = 6 years, UP TO 2 consecutive terms. Remember: the President's term is the strictest in the Constitution.

subject: General Information
question: What is the term of office of a Senator under the 1987 Philippine Constitution, and how many consecutive terms may a Senator serve?

choices.text: Three years; not more than three consecutive terms
Six years; not more than two consecutive terms
Four years; not more than two consecutive terms
Six years; not more than three consecutive terms
Six years; not more than one consecutive term

explanation: Article VI, Section 4 sets the senatorial term at six years. The same provision caps consecutive service at two terms, meaning after 12 consecutive years a Senator must sit out at least one full term before running again. This limit was absent under the 1935 Constitution, which Marcos exploited. The staggered nature of Senate elections — only half the 24-seat chamber is elected every three years — ensures continuity of institutional knowledge while still rotating membership.

distractorExplanations.A: Three-year terms with three-consecutive-term limits describe members of the House of Representatives and local officials, not Senators. Mixing up the legislative chambers is one of the most common CSE mistakes.
distractorExplanations.C: Four-year terms are not found anywhere in the 1987 Philippine legislative structure. Both senators and representatives have either six- or three-year terms.
distractorExplanations.D: The six-year term is correct, but the limit is two consecutive terms — not three. After two consecutive terms (12 years), the Senator must rest before running again.
distractorExplanations.E: Applying the presidential single-term rule to senators; senators may serve up to two consecutive six-year terms before being required to sit out — not just one.

tip.label: Exam Tip
tip.text: Senate = 6 years, max 2 consecutive terms (12 years total before rest). House = 3 years, max 3 consecutive terms (9 years total). Both = 24 senators, up to 250+ representatives.

subject: General Information
question: Under the 1987 Constitution, what is the minimum age requirement to vote in Philippine elections?

choices.text: 21 years old
18 years old
15 years old
16 years old
17 years old

explanation: Article V, Section 1 grants suffrage to all citizens 'who are at least eighteen years of age' and who have resided in the Philippines for at least one year, and in the place they propose to vote for at least six months. Critically, the same provision abolishes literacy, property, and other substantive tests for voting — a significant democratic advance over older constitutions that restricted the franchise. The age was lowered from 21 years (under the 1935 Constitution) to 18 in the 1973 Constitution and retained in 1987.

distractorExplanations.A: 21 was the voting age under the 1935 Constitution and remained so until 1973. The 1987 Constitution retained the lower age of 18 enacted during the Marcos era but kept it because it was a genuinely inclusive reform.
distractorExplanations.C: 15 years old is the minimum age for membership in the Sangguniang Kabataan (SK), a youth governance body under the Local Government Code — not the minimum age for regular suffrage.
distractorExplanations.D: 16 is the voting age in some countries (e.g., Austria, Scotland), but not in the Philippines. The Philippine Constitution is clear: the threshold is 18.
distractorExplanations.E: Splitting the difference between 16 (which some countries allow) and 18; the 1987 Constitution fixed the voting age at 18, reducing it from the previous 21-year requirement of the 1935 Constitution.

tip.label: Remember
tip.text: Voting age = 18. SK membership = 15–24. No literacy or property test for voting under Art. V, Sec. 1.

subject: General Information
question: Which body has the exclusive power to initiate all cases of impeachment under the 1987 Philippine Constitution?

choices.text: The Senate
The Supreme Court
The Ombudsman
The Office of the Solicitor General
The House of Representatives

explanation: Article XI, Section 3(1) is explicit: 'The House of Representatives shall have the exclusive power to initiate all cases of impeachment.' The Senate's role in impeachment is equally clear but different — it has 'the sole power to try and decide all cases of impeachment' (Sec. 3(6)). Think of the House as the grand jury (it files the complaint/articles) and the Senate as the trial court (it holds the actual trial and renders judgment). A two-thirds vote of all Senate members is needed for conviction.

distractorExplanations.A: The Senate tries and decides impeachment cases — it does not initiate them. This is a classic swap error on the CSE: remember, initiate = House; try = Senate.
distractorExplanations.B: The Supreme Court is itself subject to impeachment (the Chief Justice and Associate Justices are impeachable officials). It would be a conflict of interest for the Court to initiate its own impeachment proceedings.
distractorExplanations.C: The Ombudsman investigates and prosecutes public officials for criminal and administrative offenses, but the power to initiate impeachment belongs exclusively to the House of Representatives, not the Ombudsman.
distractorExplanations.D: The Solicitor General represents the government in court but has no impeachment power; Art. XI Sec. 3 exclusively vests the power to initiate impeachment in the House of Representatives.

tip.label: Mnemonic
tip.text: H-I-T: House Initiates, Senate Tries. Two-thirds of all Senate members needed to convict and remove.

subject: General Information
question: Under the 1987 Philippine Constitution, which article contains the Bill of Rights?

choices.text: Article II
Article IV
Article III
Article V
Article VI

explanation: The Bill of Rights is found in Article III of the 1987 Constitution and contains 22 sections spanning due process, equal protection, freedom of speech and the press, privacy of correspondence, the right against unreasonable searches and seizures, the rights of the accused, and the prohibition against torture and solitary confinement. Article II is the Declaration of Principles and State Policies, Article IV covers Citizenship, and Article V covers Suffrage. Knowing which article contains which topic is a standard CSE question type.

distractorExplanations.A: Article II covers the Declaration of Principles and State Policies — foundational policy statements about the state's character and goals, not specific individual rights enforceable in court.
distractorExplanations.B: Article IV covers Citizenship — who is a Filipino citizen and how citizenship is acquired or lost. It has nothing to do with individual rights against the government.
distractorExplanations.D: Article V covers Suffrage — the right to vote and the qualifications of voters. Suffrage is related to rights but is a separate article from the Bill of Rights proper.
distractorExplanations.E: Article VI establishes the Legislative Department (Congress), not the Bill of Rights; the Bill of Rights is contained in Article III.

tip.label: Constitution Reminder
tip.text: Article I = Territory, II = Principles, III = Bill of Rights, IV = Citizenship, V = Suffrage. Think: 'I can Try Counting Sections' (I, II, III, IV, V).

subject: General Information
question: Under the 1987 Philippine Constitution, who appoints the members of the Supreme Court?

choices.text: The President, upon recommendation of the Judicial and Bar Council
The Commission on Appointments
The Congress, by a majority vote of both chambers
The incumbent Chief Justice
The President, confirmed by the Commission on Appointments

explanation: Article VIII, Section 9 establishes that members of the Supreme Court shall be 'appointed by the President from a list of at least three nominees prepared by the Judicial and Bar Council (JBC) for every vacancy.' The JBC — a constitutionally created body composed of the Chief Justice, the Secretary of Justice, a representative of Congress, members of the Integrated Bar, professors of law, a retired Supreme Court justice, and a private sector representative — screens candidates to depoliticize judicial appointments. Crucially, Supreme Court appointments do not pass through the Commission on Appointments.

distractorExplanations.B: The Commission on Appointments only confirms certain executive appointments (e.g., heads of executive departments, ambassadors, military officers). By explicit constitutional design, judicial appointments are made without CA confirmation to keep the judiciary independent.
distractorExplanations.C: Congress plays no direct role in confirming Supreme Court justices under the 1987 Constitution. This was a deliberate change from practices under prior constitutional arrangements.
distractorExplanations.D: The Chief Justice has no power to appoint fellow justices. The appointment power belongs to the President, constrained by the JBC's shortlist.
distractorExplanations.E: Members of the Supreme Court are appointed by the President upon JBC recommendation but do NOT require confirmation by the Commission on Appointments; Art. VIII Sec. 9 explicitly exempts judicial appointments from CA confirmation.

tip.label: Exam Tip
tip.text: JBC shortlist → President appoints → No CA confirmation needed. This is one of the most tested separation-of-powers questions on the CSE.

subject: General Information
question: Which of the following bodies is one of the three independent Constitutional Commissions created under Article IX of the 1987 Philippine Constitution?

choices.text: Commission on Appointments
Commission on Human Rights
Civil Service Commission
Office of the Ombudsman
Sandiganbayan

explanation: Article IX of the 1987 Constitution creates exactly three independent Constitutional Commissions: the Civil Service Commission (Art. IX-B), the Commission on Elections (Art. IX-C), and the Commission on Audit (Art. IX-D). They share fiscal autonomy and independence safeguards. Other constitutional bodies exist — the Ombudsman under Article XI, the Commission on Human Rights under Article XIII — but they are not Article IX Constitutional Commissions, and the Commission on Appointments is a body of Congress under Article VI, not a commission of the civil service at all.

distractorExplanations.A: The Commission on Appointments is a congressional body under Article VI, Section 18 — it confirms presidential appointments and is not an Article IX commission.
distractorExplanations.B: The Commission on Human Rights is created by Article XIII, Section 17 — constitutionally mandated, but deliberately not one of the three Article IX Constitutional Commissions.
distractorExplanations.D: The Office of the Ombudsman is established under Article XI (Accountability of Public Officers) — independent, but not an Article IX Constitutional Commission.
distractorExplanations.E: The Sandiganbayan is an anti-graft court created by law pursuant to Article XI, Section 4 — a court, not a constitutional commission.

tip.label: Mnemonic
tip.text: 3 Constitutional Commissions = CSC + COMELEC + COA. The Commission on Appointments is a legislative body — it confirms appointments, it does not belong to Art. IX.

subject: General Information
question: Under the 1987 Philippine Constitution, what does the principle of civilian supremacy over the military mean in practice?

choices.text: The President, as commander-in-chief, may overrule Supreme Court decisions on military matters
Civilian authority is, at all times, supreme over the military, and the AFP's goal is to secure sovereignty and territorial integrity
The military may take over government functions during national emergencies declared by Congress
Soldiers on active duty may hold cabinet positions in the executive branch
The President, as commander-in-chief, may suspend civilian courts during wartime and replace them with military tribunals.

explanation: Article II, Section 3 enshrines civilian supremacy: 'Civilian authority is, at all times, supreme over the military. The Armed Forces of the Philippines is the protector of the people and the State. Its goal is to secure the sovereignty of the State and the integrity of the national territory.' This provision was written with Marcos's militarized dictatorship fresh in memory. It means the AFP answers to civilian leadership — the President as Commander-in-Chief, and ultimately to the constitutional order — and may never seize state power for itself.

distractorExplanations.A: The President's commander-in-chief power does not allow overruling the Supreme Court. The three branches remain co-equal; civilian supremacy over the military does not collapse the separation of powers among civilian institutions.
distractorExplanations.C: The Constitution does not allow the military to take over government functions even during emergencies. Emergency powers are granted to the President (a civilian), not the military, and even then are subject to strict congressional and judicial checks.
distractorExplanations.D: Active military officers may not hold civilian positions unless specifically authorized by law. The Constitution prohibits the military from straying into civilian governance roles.
distractorExplanations.E: Art. II Sec. 3 affirms permanent civilian supremacy; courts cannot be replaced by military tribunals at the President's discretion — judicial power remains with the Judiciary even during martial law (subject to judicial review).

tip.label: Historical Note
tip.text: Art. II, Sec. 3 was crafted in direct response to the Marcos era. It was the framers' way of saying: never again shall the military dominate civilian life.

subject: General Information
question: Which of the following is NOT a mode of acquiring Filipino citizenship under the 1987 Philippine Constitution?

choices.text: By marriage to a Filipino citizen
By birth to a Filipino father or mother
By naturalization in accordance with law
Those born before January 17, 1973 of Filipino mothers who elected Philippine citizenship upon reaching the age of majority
Being a citizen of the Philippines at the time of the adoption of the 1987 Constitution

explanation: Article IV, Section 1 of the 1987 Constitution lists who are Filipino citizens: (1) those born of Filipino fathers or mothers; (2) those born before January 17, 1973 of Filipino mothers who elected citizenship upon majority; (3) those who are citizens at adoption of the 1987 Constitution; and (4) naturalized citizens. Marriage to a Filipino does NOT automatically confer citizenship — a foreign spouse must undergo naturalization. This trips up many examinees who assume that marrying a Filipino is an automatic path to citizenship.

distractorExplanations.B: Birth to at least one Filipino parent (father or mother) is the primary mode of citizenship acquisition under the jus sanguinis principle. This is the most common way Filipinos acquire citizenship.
distractorExplanations.C: Naturalization — the legal process by which a foreigner applies for and is granted citizenship — is expressly recognized in Art. IV, Sec. 1(4) and governed by Commonwealth Act No. 473 and other statutes.
distractorExplanations.D: This is a transitional provision that recognized the citizenship of those born before January 17, 1973 (the 1973 Constitution's adoption date) of Filipino mothers, who under old law needed to elect citizenship at majority. It is expressly listed in Art. IV, Sec. 1(3).
distractorExplanations.E: Article IV, Section 1(1) expressly lists citizens at the adoption of the Constitution — it IS a recognized mode, so it cannot be the exception.

tip.label: Exam Tip
tip.text: Marriage does NOT automatically make you Filipino. A foreign spouse must naturalize. This distinction is almost always tested.

subject: General Information
question: Under the 1987 Philippine Constitution, what is the required Filipino equity in the exploration and development of natural resources?

choices.text: At least 51%
100% Filipino-owned only
At least 70%
At least 60%
At least 75%

explanation: Article XII, Section 2 of the Constitution vests ownership of all natural resources in the State and requires that exploration, development, and utilization shall be 'under the full control and supervision of the State.' For corporations, at least 60% of capital must be Filipino-owned. The same 60-40 Filipino-foreign ratio applies to public utilities and mass media ownership under related constitutional provisions. This principle — that the nation's wealth belongs to Filipinos first — is a cornerstone of economic nationalism in the Constitution.

distractorExplanations.A: 51% is the minimum Filipino equity required for certain other activities (e.g., some retail trade businesses), not for natural resource exploration. The natural resources provision specifically requires 60%.
distractorExplanations.B: The Constitution does not require 100% Filipino ownership of natural resource enterprises. It allows joint ventures with foreign investors, subject to the 60-40 equity floor in favor of Filipinos.
distractorExplanations.C: 70% is not cited in the Constitution for this purpose. The constitutional threshold for Filipino equity in natural resource utilization is specifically 60%.
distractorExplanations.E: Confusing the 60% Filipino-ownership requirement for public utilities with a stricter 75% threshold; Art. XII Sec. 11 sets the floor at 60%, not 75%.

tip.label: Constitution Reminder
tip.text: Natural resources, public utilities, mass media = 60% Filipino minimum. Think: 60/40 is the constitutional equity rule for 'strategic' sectors.

subject: General Information
question: Under the 1987 Constitution, who succeeds the President in case of death, permanent disability, removal from office, or resignation?

choices.text: The Senate President
The Speaker of the House
The Vice-President
The Chief Justice of the Supreme Court
The Executive Secretary

explanation: Article VII, Section 8 is clear: 'In case of death, permanent disability, removal from office, or resignation of the President, the Vice-President shall become the President.' If both the President and Vice-President are unable to serve, the Senate President (or in his inability, the Speaker of the House) acts as President until either the President or Vice-President is able to serve. This line of succession was carefully designed to maintain continuity of government. The Vice-President is thus a constitutional safety valve, not merely a ceremonial role.

distractorExplanations.A: The Senate President is third in line — acting only when both the President and Vice-President cannot serve. Confusing the second and third in line is a common error.
distractorExplanations.B: The Speaker of the House is fourth in the line of succession, stepping in only if the Senate President is also unavailable. The Speaker does not succeed directly upon the President's vacancy.
distractorExplanations.D: The Chief Justice administers the oath of office but does not succeed to the presidency. Judicial and executive powers remain strictly separate.
distractorExplanations.E: The Executive Secretary is a cabinet official with no constitutional line of succession to the presidency; Art. VII Sec. 8 designates the Vice-President as the first in the line of succession.

tip.label: Mnemonic
tip.text: Succession order: VP → Senate President → Speaker of the House. Remember: 'Very Smart People' (VP, Senate President, Speaker) in order.

subject: General Information
question: Under the 1987 Philippine Constitution, what does the due process clause guarantee?

choices.text: That all persons shall have the right to a speedy trial regardless of the offense charged
That persons accused of crimes shall be presumed guilty until proven innocent
That no person shall be deprived of life, liberty, or property without due process of law
That freedom of speech may never be restricted under any circumstances
That no person shall be searched or arrested without a warrant issued by a judge.

explanation: Article III, Section 1 of the Bill of Rights states: 'No person shall be deprived of life, liberty, or property without due process of law, nor shall any person be denied the equal protection of the laws.' Due process has two aspects: procedural (the government must follow fair procedures before depriving someone of rights) and substantive (laws must themselves be fair, reasonable, and just). This is one of the most powerful protections in the Constitution — it constrains not just how the government acts, but what the government may do.

distractorExplanations.A: The right to a speedy trial is a distinct right found in Article III, Section 14. It is related to due process but not the same as the due process clause itself.
distractorExplanations.B: The exact opposite is true: Article III, Section 14(2) establishes that 'In all criminal prosecutions, the accused shall be presumed innocent until the contrary is proved.' Presumption of innocence is a cornerstone of the Philippine criminal justice system.
distractorExplanations.D: Freedom of speech (Art. III, Sec. 4) can be regulated under the clear-and-present-danger test and other balancing frameworks. No constitutional right is absolute, including free speech.
distractorExplanations.E: The warrant requirement (Art. III Sec. 2) is a separate provision from the due process clause (Sec. 1); this distractor conflates two distinct Bill of Rights sections — Sec. 1 is the due process/equal protection provision, not the search-and-seizure rule.

tip.label: Constitution Reminder
tip.text: Art. III, Sec. 1: No deprivation of LIFE, LIBERTY, or PROPERTY without due process. Two types: Procedural (fair process) and Substantive (fair law).

subject: General Information
question: Under the 1987 Philippine Constitution, who exercises general supervision over local government units?

choices.text: The Department of the Interior and Local Government
The President of the Philippines
The Regional Development Council
The Commission on Elections
The Secretary of the Interior and Local Government

explanation: Article X, Section 4 vests the power of general supervision over local governments in the President: 'The President of the Philippines shall exercise general supervision over local governments.' Supervision is different from control — a supervising authority ensures that LGUs act within their prescribed powers, but cannot substitute its judgment for the LGU's. The DILG Secretary exercises this supervisory power as the President's alter ego, but the constitutional authority belongs to the President.

distractorExplanations.A: The DILG exercises supervision over LGUs as a delegate of the President — it is the executive department through which the President's supervisory power is operationalized — but the constitutional authority itself vests in the President.
distractorExplanations.C: Regional Development Councils are planning and coordinating bodies under the Constitution's Article X, Sec. 14. They do not have supervisory authority over LGUs.
distractorExplanations.D: COMELEC supervises elections involving LGUs but has no general supervisory authority over local government operations and governance.
distractorExplanations.E: The DILG Secretary assists in supervising LGUs but does not personally exercise the constitutional supervisory power over local governments; Art. X Sec. 4 vests that power directly in the President.

tip.label: Constitution Reminder
tip.text: Art. X, Sec. 4: President exercises GENERAL SUPERVISION (not control) over LGUs. DILG acts as the President's agent. 'Supervision' means checking legality, not directing policy.

subject: General Information
question: Under the 1987 Philippine Constitution, what does the State policy on social justice require?

choices.text: The State shall eliminate inequality by redistributing all private wealth
The State shall promote social justice in all phases of national development to reduce inequalities
The State shall guarantee equal income for all citizens regardless of occupation
The State shall abolish private ownership of land and transfer it to farmer beneficiaries
The State shall give priority to the rights of capital over labour in all economic decisions.

explanation: Article II, Section 10 declares: 'The State shall promote social justice in all phases of national development.' Social justice under the Constitution is not about eliminating all distinctions or guaranteeing equal outcomes — it is about giving those with less in life more in law. Article XIII (Social Justice and Human Rights) develops this further, covering labor, agrarian reform, urban land reform, health, women, and people's organizations. The goal is to reduce political, economic, and social inequality through positive State action — not wholesale nationalization or confiscation.

distractorExplanations.A: The Constitution does not mandate redistribution of all private wealth. It protects private property under the Bill of Rights while promoting a more equitable distribution through social justice programs.
distractorExplanations.C: The Constitution guarantees equal protection of the law (Art. III, Sec. 1), not equal income. Socioeconomic outcomes are influenced, not equalized, by social justice policy.
distractorExplanations.D: Agrarian reform is one component of social justice (Art. XIII, Sec. 4), but it is targeted at agricultural land and involves just compensation — not wholesale abolition of private ownership.
distractorExplanations.E: Art. XIII (Social Justice) and Art. II Sec. 18 affirm that labour is a primary social economic force; the Constitution does not subordinate labour rights to capital — it mandates social justice to reduce inequality.

tip.label: Remember
tip.text: Social justice = giving those who have LESS in life MORE in law. It is a State obligation across ALL phases of development, not just economic policy.

reference: 1987 Constitution, Art. II, Sec. 10; Art. XIII

subject: General Information
question: Under the 1987 Philippine Constitution, what is the composition of the Senate of the Philippines?

choices.text: 12 Senators elected by district, 12 appointed by the President
30 Senators elected at large
24 Senators, half elected at large and half by region
24 Senators elected at large by qualified voters of the Philippines
20 Senators elected at large by qualified voters of the Philippines

explanation: Article VI, Section 2 provides: 'The Senate shall be composed of twenty-four Senators who shall be elected at large by the qualified voters of the Philippines.' 'At large' means they represent the entire nation — not a district or region — making the Senate a truly national chamber. Elections are staggered: 12 Senators are elected every three years. This design gives Senators a nationwide constituency, theoretically making them less susceptible to narrow local interests compared to House members.

distractorExplanations.A: No Senators are appointed. Presidential appointment of Senators was a feature of some earlier governance periods but is explicitly absent from the 1987 Constitution. All 24 are elected.
distractorExplanations.B: The Senate has exactly 24 members — not 30. Thirty is sometimes confused with the number of members in the Supreme Court (15 justices) or misremembered from other contexts.
distractorExplanations.C: Senators are elected at large — meaning all 24 represent the whole Philippines, not half-and-half by national or regional constituencies.
distractorExplanations.E: Confusing 20 with the constitutionally mandated 24; Art. VI Sec. 2 explicitly states 24 senators elected at large — the number 20 has no constitutional basis.

tip.label: Exam Tip
tip.text: Senate = 24 members, elected AT LARGE, 12 elected every 3 years (staggered). House = up to 250+ members, elected by district plus party-list representatives.

subject: General Information
question: Under the 1987 Philippine Constitution, what is the composition of the Supreme Court?

choices.text: A Chief Justice and 14 Associate Justices
A Chief Justice and 12 Associate Justices
A Chief Justice and 16 Associate Justices
A Chief Justice and 8 Associate Justices
A Chief Justice and 10 Associate Justices

explanation: Article VIII, Section 4(1) states: 'The Supreme Court shall be composed of a Chief Justice and fourteen Associate Justices.' This gives the Court a total membership of 15, which matters because a quorum (minimum for the Court to transact business) is eight members. All constitutional questions, cases involving the constitutionality of laws, and decisions declaring a law unconstitutional require the concurrence of a majority of all members who actually participated — not just those present. The Court sits either en banc (all 15) or in divisions (of three, five, or seven).

distractorExplanations.B: 12 Associate Justices gives a total of 13 — that is not the constitutional number. This might be confused with the Court of Appeals division size or misremembered.
distractorExplanations.C: 16 Associate Justices (total of 17) is not the constitutional composition. The Constitution is specific: 15 total, 1 Chief Justice + 14 Associates.
distractorExplanations.D: 8 Associate Justices is too few. The full bench of 15 allows the Court to split into smaller divisions while retaining a large enough en banc for constitutional cases.
distractorExplanations.E: Confusing the Supreme Court composition with that of a lower collegiate court; Art. VIII Sec. 4 fixes the Supreme Court at a Chief Justice and 14 Associate Justices for a total of 15 members.

tip.label: Mnemonic
tip.text: Supreme Court = 1 Chief + 14 Associates = 15 total. Think '15' as in 'SC15.' Quorum = 8 (a majority of 15).

subject: General Information
question: Under Article IX-B of the 1987 Constitution, appointments in the civil service shall be made according to what primary criterion?

choices.text: Competitive examination
Presidential appointment without other requirements
Educational attainment alone
Seniority and length of service
Appointment by the Civil Service Commission based on agency recommendation

explanation: Article IX-B, Section 2(2) mandates that 'Appointments in the civil service shall be made only according to merit and fitness to be determined, as far as practicable, and except to positions which are policy-determining, primarily confidential, or highly technical, by competitive examination.' This merit-and-fitness rule is why the Civil Service Exam exists — it depoliticizes government hiring by ensuring that public positions go to those who earn them, not those with political connections. It is one of the most direct constitutional foundations of the CSE system that examinees are sitting for.

distractorExplanations.B: Presidential appointment is the mode for certain high-level positions (e.g., department secretaries, ambassadors), but the Constitution requires those appointments to be based on merit, not discretion alone.
distractorExplanations.C: Educational attainment is one factor in merit assessment but is not by itself the constitutional standard. The Constitution prescribes competitive examination as the primary metric, supplemented by education and experience for non-exam positions.
distractorExplanations.D: Seniority matters for promotions within the civil service, but the primary constitutional basis for initial appointment is merit and fitness determined by competitive examination, not length of service.
distractorExplanations.E: The CSC does not make appointments; it sets standards and administers examinations. Appointments are made by the appointing authority in each agency, and the general rule for entry is passage of the competitive civil service examination.

tip.label: Remember
tip.text: The Civil Service Exam you're taking exists because of Art. IX-B, Sec. 2(2). Appointments must follow merit — this is constitutional, not just policy.

subject: General Information
question: The 1987 Constitution, Article III, Section 4, prohibits the passage of any law abridging which of the following rights?

choices.text: The right to bear arms
The right to education and literacy
The right to economic livelihood and employment
The freedom of speech, of expression, or of the press, or the right of the people peaceably to assemble and petition the Government
The right to privacy of communication and correspondence

explanation: Article III, Section 4 declares: 'No law shall be passed abridging the freedom of speech, of expression, or of the press, or the right of the people peaceably to assemble and to petition the government for redress of grievances.' These clustered freedoms — speech, expression, press, assembly, and petition — are known as the 'preferred freedoms' because they are essential to democracy itself. Without these rights, citizens cannot critique their government, organize politically, or advocate for change. They are therefore subject to the strictest judicial scrutiny when the government attempts to regulate them.

distractorExplanations.A: The right to bear arms is not in the 1987 Philippine Constitution. Unlike the U.S. Second Amendment, the Philippine Bill of Rights contains no such provision. Firearms ownership in the Philippines is a statutory — not constitutional — matter.
distractorExplanations.B: The right to education is found in Article XIV, not Article III. It is a positive right requiring State action, not a freedom from government interference like the Art. III, Sec. 4 freedoms.
distractorExplanations.C: The right to livelihood is recognized in jurisprudence and some social justice provisions, but it is not specifically protected by Article III, Section 4. That section protects political/expressive freedoms.
distractorExplanations.E: Privacy of communication (Art. III Sec. 3) is a separate provision from freedom of expression (Sec. 4); the question's key is specifically the freedom of speech/expression/press/assembly cluster under Sec. 4.

tip.label: Constitution Reminder
tip.text: Art. III, Sec. 4 protects FIVE freedoms: speech, expression, press, peaceful assembly, and petition. These are called 'preferred freedoms' because democracy cannot survive without them.

subject: General Information
question: Under Article IX-B of the 1987 Constitution, what are the qualifications for a member of the Civil Service Commission?

choices.text: At least 35 years of age with proven capacity for public administration
At least 40 years of age with at least 10 years of legal practice
At least 45 years of age with 15 years of civil service experience
At least 30 years of age with a master's degree in public administration
At least 40 years of age with at least 15 years of government service

explanation: Article IX-B, Section 1(1) prescribes that CSC commissioners must be 'natural-born citizens of the Philippines and, at the time of their appointment, are at least thirty-five years of age, with proven capacity for public administration, and must not have been candidates for any elective position in the elections immediately preceding their appointment.' Note that the qualification does not require a specific professional license like the law-practice requirement for COMELEC or COA, reflecting the CSC's broader mandate over all civil servants regardless of professional background.

distractorExplanations.B: The 40-year age minimum and legal practice requirement describe qualifications for members of COMELEC (Art. IX-C, Sec. 1), not the CSC. This is a classic cross-commission confusion on the CSE.
distractorExplanations.C: 45 years of age with civil service experience is not the constitutional standard for any of the three commissions. Do not confuse personal intuition with actual constitutional text.
distractorExplanations.D: The Constitution does not require a master's degree for CSC membership. It requires 'proven capacity for public administration' — a broader, less specific standard than a degree requirement.
distractorExplanations.E: Combining the age requirement from one wrong option with the experience figure from another; Art. IX-B Sec. 1 requires only at least 35 years of age and proven capacity for public administration — it does not specify years of government service.

tip.label: Exam Tip
tip.text: CSC: 35 years old + proven capacity for public administration. COMELEC: 40 years + law practice. COA: 40 years + CPA or law. Don't mix these up — it's a guaranteed CSE question.

subject: General Information
question: Article VII, Section 4 of the 1987 Constitution states that a person who has served as President for more than four years is eligible to run for President again. Is this statement correct?

choices.text: Yes, after sitting out one term
No, such a person is never qualified for election to the presidency
Yes, if endorsed by a political party
Yes, since the constitutional prohibition applies only to duly-elected Presidents
No, such a person may only run for senator or local official, never for the presidency.

explanation: Article VII, Section 4 of the 1987 Constitution is unambiguous: 'No person who has succeeded as President and has served as such for more than four years shall be qualified for election to the same office at any time.' The key phrase is 'at any time' — there is no cooling-off period after which eligibility is restored. If a Vice-President succeeds to the presidency and serves more than four years, that person is permanently barred from the presidency. This prevents circumvention of the one-term limit through succession.

distractorExplanations.A: There is no one-term sitting-out period that restores eligibility. The disqualification under Sec. 4 is permanent — 'at any time' leaves no room for a comeback election.
distractorExplanations.C: Political party endorsement cannot override a constitutional disqualification. COMELEC would disqualify such a candidate regardless of party backing.
distractorExplanations.D: The prohibition applies not only to elected Presidents but also to those who succeed to the office and serve more than four years. The Constitution explicitly closes this loophole.
distractorExplanations.E: Art. VII Sec. 4 prohibits any person who has served as president for more than four years from ever running for president again; it does not restrict them from seeking other offices — the prohibition is specifically and exclusively about the presidency.

tip.label: Constitution Reminder
tip.text: Succeeded to presidency + served MORE than 4 years = NEVER eligible for election to presidency again. If served 4 years or LESS as successor, they may run once for a full term.

subject: General Information
question: Under Article III, Section 7 of the 1987 Constitution, what is the scope of the right of the people to information on matters of public concern?

choices.text: Only published government reports and audited financial statements
All government communications including those classified as state secrets
Only court decisions and legislative records
Official records and documents pertaining to official acts, transactions, or decisions, as well as government research data used as basis for policy development
All government records including those involving national security and military intelligence

explanation: Article III, Section 7 guarantees 'the right of the people to information on matters of public concern,' with access to 'official records, and to documents and papers pertaining to official acts, transactions, or decisions, as well as to government research data used as basis for policy development.' This right is not absolute — the same provision recognizes that access shall be 'afforded the citizen, subject to such limitations as may be provided by law.' Classified state secrets, diplomatic correspondence, and privileged communications may be withheld under law, but the default is transparency.

distractorExplanations.A: The right to information covers far more than published reports — it extends to unpublished records, transaction documents, and data underlying policy decisions. Limiting it to published materials would hollow out the guarantee.
distractorExplanations.B: State secrets and classified information are among the recognized exceptions to the right to information. The Constitution itself acknowledges that limitations may be set by law for legitimate governmental interests.
distractorExplanations.C: Limiting access only to court and legislative records would exclude the vast bulk of executive branch documents — contracts, permits, internal memos — that affect public welfare most directly.
distractorExplanations.E: Art. III Sec. 7 provides that access to information may be limited by law for national security and other legitimate state interests; not all records are unrestricted — classified security information is a recognised exception.

tip.label: Constitution Reminder
tip.text: Art. III, Sec. 7: Right to information on matters of public concern. Covers official records, transactions, decisions, and policy data — subject to legal limitations. Paired with the right to petition (Sec. 4).

subject: General Information
question: What is the declared policy of the State under Section 2 of Republic Act No. 6713?

choices.text: To promote efficiency and reduce costs in government operations
To impose strict criminal penalties for all forms of corruption
To professionalize the civil service through mandatory examinations
To establish a merit and fitness system for promotion within the civil service
To promote a high standard of ethics in public service and require public officials to uphold public interest over personal interest

explanation: Section 2 of RA 6713 (Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Officials and Employees) declares it the State policy 'to promote a high standard of ethics in public service. Public officials and employees shall at all times be accountable to the people and shall discharge their duties with utmost responsibility, integrity, competence, and loyalty, act with patriotism and justice, lead modest lives, and uphold public interest over and above personal interest.' This is the moral north star of the entire law — accountability and ethics, not efficiency or punishments alone, are the primary focus.

distractorExplanations.A: Efficiency is a desirable quality in public service, but it is not the declared State policy under Section 2 of RA 6713. The law's primary concern is ethics and accountability, not cost reduction.
distractorExplanations.B: While RA 6713 does include administrative penalties (Section 11), its declared policy is not primarily punitive — it is preventive and character-forming. Criminal penalties for corruption are found in other laws (e.g., RA 3019, the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act).
distractorExplanations.C: Professionalization of the civil service through examinations is the mandate of the Civil Service Commission under the Constitution and RA 2260 — not the declared policy of RA 6713, which focuses specifically on ethical standards.
distractorExplanations.D: A merit-and-fitness promotion system is the domain of the Civil Service Commission and related laws; RA 6713's stated policy is the promotion of high ethical standards and responsiveness to the public — not promotion procedures.

tip.label: Law Reminder
tip.text: RA 6713 = 'Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards.' Its heart is Section 2: high ethics, accountability, public interest over personal interest. Think ETHICS first, penalties second.

subject: General Information
question: Under RA 6713, which norm of conduct requires public officials and employees to 'lead modest lives appropriate to their positions and income' and prohibits extravagant display of wealth?

choices.text: Justness and sincerity
Commitment to public interest
Simple living
Professionalism
Transparency

explanation: Section 4(A)(h) of RA 6713 prescribes the norm of 'Simple Living': public officials and employees shall lead lives modest and appropriate to their positions and income. They shall not indulge in extravagant or ostentatious display of wealth in any form. This norm addresses a very Filipino concern — the conspicuous consumption by some public officials while in office, financed by questionable sources. Simple living is both an ethical standard and an anti-corruption signal: a lifestyle inconsistent with declared income raises red flags.

distractorExplanations.A: Justness and sincerity (Sec. 4(A)(c)) requires officials to act with justice and sincerity, not to seek personal gain. It is about honesty and fairness in dealings, not lifestyle standards.
distractorExplanations.B: Commitment to public interest (Sec. 4(A)(a)) obliges officials to devote themselves to public service and not use official position for private advantage — an important but different norm from lifestyle management.
distractorExplanations.D: Professionalism (Sec. 4(A)(b)) requires carrying out duties with excellence and skill. It concerns job performance, not the official's personal lifestyle or display of wealth.
distractorExplanations.E: While transparency is a core value in Philippine governance, 'transparency' is not one of the eight norms of conduct enumerated in Sec. 4 of RA 6713; the correct norm related to the question is simple living.

tip.label: Mnemonic
tip.text: RA 6713 Norms of Conduct include: Commitment to Public Interest, Professionalism, Justness & Sincerity, Political Neutrality, Responsiveness, Nationalism & Patriotism, Commitment to Democracy, Simple Living. Mnemonic: 'Can Pigs Jump? Please Note Results Soon.'

subject: General Information
question: Under RA 6713, which agency has the primary responsibility for the administration and enforcement of the Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards?

choices.text: The Office of the Ombudsman
The Civil Service Commission
The Department of Justice
The Office of the President
The Presidential Commission on Good Government (PCGG)

explanation: Section 12 of RA 6713 designates the Civil Service Commission (CSC) as the primary agency responsible for administering and implementing the Code. The CSC has the power to issue rules and regulations, investigate violations, and impose administrative sanctions. This is consistent with the CSC's constitutional mandate to administer the civil service system — it is the natural enforcer of ethical standards for government workers. The Ombudsman, by contrast, has jurisdiction over criminal and more serious administrative offenses by government officials.

distractorExplanations.A: The Office of the Ombudsman investigates and prosecutes public officials for criminal acts and grave administrative offenses, but RA 6713's primary administrative enforcement is lodged in the CSC. The Ombudsman may still take action on more serious violations.
distractorExplanations.C: The Department of Justice is the principal law agency of the government but has no specific mandate under RA 6713 for the day-to-day enforcement of ethical standards for public employees.
distractorExplanations.D: The Office of the President exercises general supervision over the executive branch but does not serve as the primary enforcement body for RA 6713. That role belongs to the CSC.
distractorExplanations.E: The PCGG was established to recover ill-gotten wealth from the Marcos era and is not the administering body of RA 6713; Sec. 11 of RA 6713 designates the Civil Service Commission as the administrator.

tip.label: Law Reminder
tip.text: RA 6713 enforcement = Civil Service Commission (primary). Sec. 12 says so explicitly. For criminal graft, it's the Ombudsman + Sandiganbayan, not the CSC.

subject: General Information
question: Under Section 8 of RA 6713, all public officials and employees are required to file a Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN). Which of the following categories is expressly EXCLUDED from this requirement?

choices.text: Permanent employees in the national government
Those who serve in an honorary capacity, laborers, and casual or temporary workers
Local government officials
Military and police personnel
Foreign nationals employed in Philippine government instrumentalities

explanation: Section 8(A) of RA 6713 states that 'All public officials and employees, except those who serve in an honorary capacity, laborers and casual or temporary workers, shall file under oath their Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth.' The exclusion is logical: honorary officials are not compensated or empowered to transact public business in ways that generate conflict-of-interest risks. Casual and temporary workers have minimal decision-making power. All others — from barangay officials to cabinet secretaries — must file the SALN annually.

distractorExplanations.A: Permanent national government employees are very much required to file SALNs. They hold stable positions with significant decision-making authority and are among the primary targets of the SALN requirement.
distractorExplanations.C: Local government officials — from barangay chairs to governors — are required to file SALNs. The law covers all levels of government, not just the national.
distractorExplanations.D: Military and police personnel are public officials and employees covered by RA 6713. They are not excluded from the SALN filing requirement.
distractorExplanations.E: RA 6713 covers public officials and employees of Philippine government agencies; foreign nationals may be employed in certain capacities but the law's exemption clause (Sec. 8) lists honorary, laborer, and casual employees — not foreign nationals as a class.

tip.label: Law Reminder
tip.text: SALN exceptions under RA 6713: honorary officials, laborers, casual/temporary workers. Everyone else files annually — on or before April 30 each year. Filing deadlines: within 30 days of assumption; April 30 annually; within 30 days of separation.

subject: General Information
question: Under Section 9 of RA 6713, when a conflict of interest arises, within how many days must a public official make a full disclosure to the appropriate authorities?

choices.text: Fifteen (15) days
Thirty (30) days
Sixty (60) days
Ninety (90) days
Forty-five (45) days

explanation: Section 9 of RA 6713 governs divestment and disclosure when a conflict of interest arises: 'A public official or employee shall, within thirty (30) days from assumption of office and within thirty (30) days after the acquisition of any personal or financial interest, make a full disclosure to the appropriate authorities.' The 30-day rule recurs throughout RA 6713 — it is also the deadline for SALN filing after assumption of office and after separation. The 30-day interval is designed to be short enough to prevent conflicts from taking root, but long enough to give officials time to identify and document their interests.

distractorExplanations.A: 15 days is not the prescribed period for conflict-of-interest disclosure under RA 6713. Fifteen days is sometimes the timeline for other government processes, but not this provision.
distractorExplanations.C: 60 days exceeds the statutory requirement. The law is stricter — 30 days is the deadline, reflecting the urgency of resolving conflicts of interest before they can influence official decisions.
distractorExplanations.D: 90 days is a common administrative deadline (e.g., the 90-day period for the CSC to issue implementing rules), but not the conflict-of-interest disclosure period.
distractorExplanations.E: Splitting the difference between the 30-day actual requirement and 60 days; Sec. 9 of RA 6713 prescribes exactly 30 days for divestment of business interests that conflict with official duties.

tip.label: Law Reminder
tip.text: RA 6713 loves the number 30: SALN within 30 days of assumption; SALN within 30 days of separation; conflict-of-interest disclosure within 30 days. When in doubt on RA 6713 timelines, think 30.

subject: General Information
question: RA 6713 defines 'relatives' for the purpose of prohibitions on undue favors as persons related to a public official within what degree of relationship?

choices.text: Within the third civil degree
Within the second civil degree
Within the fifth civil degree
Within the fourth civil degree
Within the sixth civil degree of consanguinity or affinity

explanation: Section 3(d) of RA 6713 defines 'relatives' as 'persons related to a public official or employee within the fourth civil degree of consanguinity or affinity.' The civil degree system measures blood or marriage proximity: first degree (parent-child, siblings), second degree (grandparent-grandchild, uncle-niece), third degree (first cousins once removed), fourth degree (first cousins). This definition is important because Section 7(b) prohibits public officials from recommending relatives within this degree for positions in government where the official can exert influence.

distractorExplanations.A: Third civil degree is narrower than the statutory definition — it would exclude first cousins who are within the fourth degree. The law deliberately draws a wider circle.
distractorExplanations.B: Second civil degree is even narrower — it would cover only very close family (grandparents, siblings' children). The law's scope extends further to prevent nepotism through more distant but still influential family ties.
distractorExplanations.C: Fifth civil degree would be broader than the statute. The law does not extend prohibitions to second cousins or beyond (fifth degree).
distractorExplanations.E: Extending the definition beyond the law's scope; Sec. 3(j) of RA 6713 defines 'relatives' as those within the fourth civil degree of consanguinity or affinity — the sixth degree is beyond this statutory boundary.

tip.label: Law Reminder
tip.text: RA 6713 'relatives' = within 4th civil degree of consanguinity or affinity. That includes: children (1st), grandchildren (2nd), great-grandchildren (3rd), and first cousins (4th). This is the anti-nepotism boundary.

subject: General Information
question: Under RA 6713, what is the norm of conduct that requires public officials to 'extend prompt, courteous, and adequate service to the public' without discrimination?

choices.text: Commitment to public interest
Nationalism and patriotism
Justness and sincerity
Accountability
Responsiveness to the public

explanation: Section 4(A)(e) prescribes 'Responsiveness to the Public': public officials must 'extend prompt, courteous, and adequate service to the public.' More specifically, they shall 'respond to letters, telegrams or other documents received within fifteen (15) working days from receipt thereof.' This norm reflects the principle that government exists to serve citizens — not the other way around. It has teeth: unresponsiveness can be cited in administrative cases. This also connects to RA 11032 (Ease of Doing Business Act), which modernizes and enforces service delivery standards.

distractorExplanations.A: Commitment to Public Interest (Sec. 4(A)(a)) requires officials to act primarily for the public good and not use their position for private advantage — it is about whose interests are served, not about the speed and quality of service delivery.
distractorExplanations.B: Nationalism and Patriotism (Sec. 4(A)(f)) obligates officials to be loyal to the Republic and promote Filipino products and services. It is about civic loyalty, not customer-service responsiveness.
distractorExplanations.C: Justness and Sincerity (Sec. 4(A)(c)) requires officials to act with justice and sincerity, avoiding acts that give undue advantages. It concerns honesty in dealings, not public service delivery standards.
distractorExplanations.D: Accountability is a fundamental governance principle but is not listed as one of the eight norms of conduct in Sec. 4 of RA 6713; the listed norms include commitment to public interest, professionalism, justness and sincerity, political neutrality, responsiveness, nationalism, integrity, and simple living.

tip.label: Law Reminder
tip.text: Responsiveness to the Public: respond within 15 working days. 'Prompt, courteous, and adequate service.' Citizens are not subjects — they are the bosses of public servants.

subject: General Information
question: Section 7(d) of RA 6713 prohibits public officials from soliciting or accepting gifts. Which of the following is NOT prohibited under this section?

choices.text: A gift of significant monetary value given during Christmas by a contractor seeking a government project
An unsolicited gift of nominal or insignificant value not given in anticipation of or in exchange for a favor from a public official
A loan extended to a public official by a company whose application is pending before his office
Any entertainment given by a person whose transaction is being officially acted upon
A token of appreciation from a former client given five years after the official's retirement

explanation: Section 7(d) of RA 6713 prohibits public officials from soliciting or accepting any gift, loan, gratuity, discount, favor, hospitality, or benefit given in anticipation of or in connection with an official act. However, the provision expressly exempts 'gifts or grants from foreign governments' approved by Congress and, by extension, gifts that are genuinely unsolicited, of nominal or insignificant value, and not given in exchange for or in anticipation of any favor or official action. The key tests are: Was it solicited? Is it valuable? Is it connected to an official transaction? If none of these apply, it may be permissible.

distractorExplanations.A: A gift from a contractor seeking a government project — regardless of timing (Christmas included) — is clearly connected to an anticipated official transaction and is prohibited under RA 6713 and anti-graft laws.
distractorExplanations.C: A loan from a company with a pending application is a classic form of prohibited benefit. Even if called a 'loan,' extending credit to an official with power over the lender's application is the kind of subtle corruption the law targets.
distractorExplanations.D: Entertainment given by a person whose transaction is being officially acted upon is expressly enumerated as prohibited. The presence of an active official connection makes even social gestures impermissible.
distractorExplanations.E: Post-retirement gifts from former clients can still fall under prohibited acts if they relate to prior official actions; only gifts of nominal value unconnected to any official act or benefit are clearly permissible under RA 6713.

tip.label: Law Reminder
tip.text: RA 6713 gift rule: Unsolicited + Nominal value + No connection to official act = OK. Solicited OR valuable OR connected to a transaction = PROHIBITED. When in doubt, decline.

subject: General Information
question: Under Section 11 of RA 6713, what is the maximum fine that may be imposed for a violation of the Code of Conduct?

choices.text: The equivalent of three months' salary
The equivalent of twelve months' salary
The equivalent of six months' salary
A fixed fine of fifty thousand pesos
The equivalent of nine months' salary

explanation: Section 11 of RA 6713 prescribes that violations shall be punished by a fine not exceeding the equivalent of six months' salary, dismissal from service, and perpetual disqualification from public office as accessory penalties. The administrative penalties under RA 6713 do not replace criminal liability — a public official may simultaneously face administrative sanctions under RA 6713 and criminal prosecution under RA 3019 (Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act) or the Revised Penal Code for the same conduct. Administrative penalties are lighter, but the reputational and career damage from dismissal is severe.

distractorExplanations.A: Three months' salary equivalent is below the maximum prescribed by law. The statute allows fines up to six months' salary — a significantly heavier financial penalty.
distractorExplanations.B: Twelve months' salary equivalent exceeds the maximum allowed under RA 6713. This might be confused with penalties under stricter anti-graft statutes.
distractorExplanations.D: RA 6713 does not prescribe a fixed peso amount as the maximum fine. The fine is indexed to the violator's salary — a salary-scaled approach that makes the penalty proportionate to the official's earnings.
distractorExplanations.E: Splitting the difference between six and twelve months' salary; Sec. 11 of RA 6713 sets the maximum fine at an amount equivalent to and not exceeding the employee's six months' salary and benefits.

tip.label: Law Reminder
tip.text: RA 6713 max fine = 6 months' salary equivalent. Plus possible dismissal and perpetual disqualification from public office. These are ADMINISTRATIVE penalties — criminal liability is separate.

subject: General Information
question: Under RA 6713, the norm of 'Nationalism and patriotism' requires public officials to do which of the following?

choices.text: Be loyal to the Republic and to the Filipino people, promote the use of Filipino products, and contribute to national development
Prioritize foreign investment and global partnerships above all else
Use English as the primary language in all official communications
Join civic organizations and attend national celebrations
Comply with all directives of their political party even when in public office.

explanation: Section 4(A)(f) prescribes 'Nationalism and Patriotism': public officials must be loyal to the Republic of the Philippines and to the Filipino people, promote the use of Filipino products, resources and technology, and 'as far as practicable, shall act to protect the dignity of the Philippines and the dignity of the Filipino.' This norm has both political (loyalty) and economic (buy Filipino) dimensions. It reflects the constitutional principle of economic nationalism and the State's duty to put Filipino interests first — including in procurement and consumption decisions by government offices.

distractorExplanations.B: Foreign investment and partnerships may serve national interests, but nationalism under RA 6713 specifically prioritizes Filipino products and resources — it is not an instruction to maximize foreign engagement.
distractorExplanations.C: The norm of nationalism does not prescribe English use — the opposite is implied, with promotion of Filipino language and products. Constitutional language policy (Art. XIV) supports Filipino as the national language.
distractorExplanations.D: Joining civic organizations and attending celebrations are not mandated by this norm. The requirement is substantive loyalty and concrete promotion of Filipino goods and dignity, not ceremonial participation.
distractorExplanations.E: RA 6713 Sec. 4(e) requires political neutrality; following partisan party directives that conflict with public duty violates this norm — public officials must prioritise public interest over political party loyalty.

tip.label: Law Reminder
tip.text: Nationalism & Patriotism norm: loyalty to the Republic + promote Filipino products. This means government offices should favor locally made goods in procurement when practicable.

subject: General Information
question: RA 6713 defines 'divestment' as which of the following?

choices.text: The temporary suspension of business interests while in public office
The declaration of all business interests in the SALN without changing ownership
The placement of private property in a blind trust managed by a third party
The formal declaration of a public official's assets and liabilities to the Civil Service Commission.
The transfer of title or disposal of interest in property by voluntarily, completely, and actually depriving oneself of ownership

explanation: Section 3(j) of RA 6713 defines 'divestment' as 'the transfer of title or disposal of interest in property by voluntarily, completely and actually depriving or dispossessing oneself of his right or title to it in favor of a person or persons other than his spouse and relatives as defined in this Act.' The key words are 'voluntarily, completely and actually' — a nominal transfer to a family member, or retaining any beneficial interest, does not qualify. Divestment is required when a public official holds interests in a business regulated by or transacting with their office, to prevent conflicts of interest.

distractorExplanations.A: Temporary suspension or placing a business 'on hold' does not constitute divestment. The law requires actual, complete transfer of ownership — pausing operations while still owning the business leaves the conflict of interest intact.
distractorExplanations.B: Declaring interests in the SALN is disclosure, not divestment. SALN filing is a transparency mechanism; divestment is a structural change in ownership designed to eliminate the conflict of interest at its source.
distractorExplanations.C: A blind trust is a common mechanism in other jurisdictions (notably the U.S.) but RA 6713 does not specifically authorize it as a substitute for divestment. The definition requires actual deprivation of ownership, not merely blind management.
distractorExplanations.D: Describing the SALN filing requirement rather than divestment; divestment under Sec. 3(d) of RA 6713 means actually transferring title or disposing of a conflicting interest — not merely declaring it.

tip.label: Law Reminder
tip.text: Divestment = ACTUAL and COMPLETE transfer of ownership. Not to spouse/relatives. Not just disclosure. 'Blind trusts' are not the Philippine standard — real divestment is required.

subject: General Information
question: Under Section 4(A)(g) of RA 6713, the norm of 'Commitment to democracy' requires public officials to do which of the following?

choices.text: Supremacy of the military in national security matters
Loyalty to their political party and its agenda above all else
Compliance with orders of the President regardless of constitutional limitations
Obedience to the directives of the head of department at all times, regardless of legality.
Supremacy of civilian authority over the military, and to put into practice the principle of sovereignty of the people

explanation: Section 4(A)(g) of RA 6713 requires public officials to 'commit to the democratic way of life and values, maintain the principle of public accountability, and manifest by deeds the supremacy of civilian authority over the military.' It also requires them to 'at all times uphold the Constitution and put loyalty to country above loyalty to persons or party.' This norm mirrors the constitutional principle of civilian supremacy in Art. II, Sec. 3 and reinforces that no official — civilian or military — may place partisan or personal loyalty above the rule of law.

distractorExplanations.A: Civilian supremacy — not military supremacy — is both the constitutional (Art. II, Sec. 3) and statutory (RA 6713, Sec. 4(A)(g)) standard. The military serves under, not over, civilian government.
distractorExplanations.B: RA 6713 explicitly says loyalty must be to country and Constitution — 'above loyalty to persons or party.' Placing party above constitutional duty violates this norm.
distractorExplanations.C: Blind obedience to presidential orders that violate the Constitution is not commitment to democracy — it is the opposite. Public officials have an independent duty to uphold the Constitution, which can override individual orders.
distractorExplanations.D: RA 6713 Sec. 4 requires public officials to uphold the Constitution and laws — obedience to unlawful orders is not a norm of conduct; officials are duty-bound to refuse unconstitutional or illegal orders.

tip.label: Law Reminder
tip.text: Commitment to Democracy: civilian over military; Constitution over persons or party. Public officials cannot hide behind 'just following orders' when those orders violate the Constitution.

subject: General Information
question: The SALN under RA 6713 requires disclosure of assets, liabilities, net worth, and financial and business interests of the public official and whose other dependents?

choices.text: All relatives within the fourth civil degree of consanguinity or affinity
All household members regardless of age or relationship
Parents and siblings of the public official
All dependents claimed in the employee's income tax return
Spouses and unmarried children under eighteen (18) years of age

explanation: Section 8 of RA 6713 specifies that the SALN must cover the public official's assets, liabilities, net worth, and financial and business interests 'including those of their spouses and of unmarried children under eighteen (18) years of age.' The scope is intentionally limited to the official's immediate household — spouse and minor children — because these family members are most likely to serve as conduits for hidden wealth. It does not extend to all relatives, parents, or adult children who live independently.

distractorExplanations.A: All relatives within the fourth civil degree would sweep in uncles, aunts, cousins, and others who live independently and are not household members subject to the official's influence. This overstates the SALN's scope.
distractorExplanations.B: Household members regardless of relationship is too broad. The law is specific: spouses and unmarried children under 18 — not household employees, boarders, or relatives who happen to live with the official.
distractorExplanations.C: Parents and siblings are not included in the SALN requirement unless they are classified as dependents as spouses or minor children, which they normally are not.
distractorExplanations.D: The income tax return's list of dependents is a different legal concept; RA 6713 Sec. 8 requires disclosure of the assets, liabilities, and net worth of the official's spouse and unmarried children under 18 — not all tax dependents.

tip.label: Law Reminder
tip.text: SALN covers: public official + SPOUSE + unmarried children under 18. Not all relatives — just the immediate nuclear family unit. Remember: Sec. 8 = nuclear family only.

subject: General Information
question: The Commission on Human Rights (CHR) of the Philippines was created under which article of the 1987 Constitution?

choices.text: Article XI (Accountability of Public Officers)
Article IX-B (Civil Service Commission)
Article III (Bill of Rights)
Article X (Local Government)
Article XIII (Social Justice and Human Rights)

explanation: Article XIII, Section 17 of the 1987 Constitution creates the Commission on Human Rights as an independent constitutional body under the article on Social Justice and Human Rights. The CHR's constitutional mandate includes investigating violations of civil and political rights, monitoring government compliance with treaty obligations, and providing legal measures for the protection of human rights. Unlike the three Constitutional Commissions (CSC, COMELEC, COA) in Article IX, the CHR has a more focused, rights-protection mandate and does not have the same fiscal and administrative independence.

distractorExplanations.A: Article XI covers accountability of public officers — impeachment, the Ombudsman, and the Sandiganbayan. The CHR is not an accountability mechanism for public officers but a rights-protection body.
distractorExplanations.B: Article IX-B covers the Civil Service Commission, one of the three independent Constitutional Commissions. The CHR is a separate body with a different mandate.
distractorExplanations.C: Article III is the Bill of Rights — it lists the rights themselves but does not create the CHR. The CHR, as the enforcer of those rights, is found in Article XIII, the Social Justice article.
distractorExplanations.D: Article X establishes the framework for local government units; the Commission on Human Rights is created under Article XIII, Sec. 17 of the 1987 Constitution.

tip.label: Constitution Reminder
tip.text: CHR = Article XIII, Sec. 17 (Social Justice & Human Rights). Not Article IX. The CHR is independent but not one of the 3 Constitutional Commissions.

subject: General Information
question: Under the 1987 Constitution, the Commission on Human Rights has the mandate to investigate violations of which category of rights?

choices.text: Civil and political rights
Economic, social, and cultural rights only
All rights including environmental and labor rights
Rights of overseas Filipino workers only
Economic, social, political, and cultural rights equally

explanation: Article XIII, Section 18(1) grants the CHR the power 'to investigate, on its own or on complaint by any party, all forms of human rights violations involving civil and political rights.' Civil and political rights are the classic first-generation human rights — the right to life, liberty, due process, equal protection, freedom of speech, and the right against torture. In the landmark Cariño v. Commission on Human Rights (1991), the Supreme Court clarified that the CHR cannot adjudicate cases (that power belongs to courts) — it investigates and recommends, but does not try and punish.

distractorExplanations.B: Economic, social, and cultural rights (the 'second generation' rights — right to work, education, health) fall under other agencies' mandates. The CHR's constitutional investigative jurisdiction covers civil and political rights.
distractorExplanations.C: Environmental and labor rights are important but are handled by DENR, DOLE, and other specialized agencies. Expanding CHR's mandate to all rights would require constitutional amendment.
distractorExplanations.D: OFW rights are an important policy concern handled by OWWA, POEA, and related agencies, but restricting the CHR to OFW rights alone dramatically understates its constitutional mandate.
distractorExplanations.E: The CHR's primary mandate under Art. XIII Sec. 18 focuses on civil and political rights violations; while it may engage with broader rights issues, its core investigatory jurisdiction is civil and political rights.

tip.label: Constitution Reminder
tip.text: CHR investigates civil and political rights violations only — not economic, social, cultural, environmental, or labor rights. And it investigates; it doesn't adjudicate (courts do that).

subject: General Information
question: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) was adopted by the United Nations General Assembly in which year?
explanation: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted by the United Nations General Assembly on December 10, 1948 — a date now celebrated globally as International Human Rights Day. The UDHR was drafted in the aftermath of World War II and the Holocaust, reflecting humanity's collective determination that the atrocities of that era must never be repeated. The Philippines was among the original signatories and voted in favor of the UDHR. 1945 was the year the UN was founded; 1966 was the year of the International Covenants on Civil and Political Rights and on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights.

distractorExplanations.A: 1945 was the year the United Nations was established (the UN Charter was signed in San Francisco on June 26, 1945). The UDHR came three years later, after the drafting process led by Eleanor Roosevelt.
distractorExplanations.B: 1966 was the year the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR) were adopted — both legally binding treaties that followed the non-binding UDHR.
distractorExplanations.C: 1950 was not a particularly significant year in international human rights law. The European Convention on Human Rights was adopted in 1950, but the UDHR had already been proclaimed in 1948.
distractorExplanations.D: Confusing the UDHR adoption date with the 1955 Bandung Conference (Asian-African Conference); the Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted by the UN General Assembly on December 10, 1948.

tip.label: Historical Note
