tip.text: Art. II, Sec. 3: 'Civilian authority is, AT ALL TIMES, supreme over the military.' No exceptions — not war, not emergency, not rebellion. The AFP protects the people; it does not rule them.

subject: General Information
question: The 1987 Philippine Constitution provides that the Supreme Court shall be composed of a Chief Justice and how many Associate Justices?

choices.text: Twelve Associate Justices
Fifteen Associate Justices
Ten Associate Justices
Fourteen Associate Justices
Thirteen Associate Justices

explanation: Article VIII, Section 4(1) of the 1987 Constitution specifies: 'The Supreme Court shall be composed of a Chief Justice and fourteen Associate Justices.' That gives the Court a total bench of 15. The Court may sit en banc — all 15 together — for the most consequential cases, particularly those involving constitutionality of laws, which require the concurrence of a majority of members who actually took part. The Court may also divide into smaller panels of three, five, or seven to handle routine appellate work. Knowing the exact number matters because the quorum (8 members) and the conviction threshold in certain actions depend directly on the total membership.

distractorExplanations.A: Twelve Associate Justices would give a total bench of 13. This is not the figure the Constitution prescribes. The Court of Appeals and Sandiganbayan also have multiple justices in dozens, which may cause confusion.
distractorExplanations.B: Fifteen is the total size of the Supreme Court — one Chief Justice plus fourteen Associates. Fifteen Associate Justices alone would make an absurdly large court of 16 total, which is not constitutional.
distractorExplanations.C: Ten Associate Justices is not the constitutional count. The Philippines has a 15-member Supreme Court, one of the larger supreme courts in Asia.
distractorExplanations.E: Thirteen is between the existing wrong options and the correct 14; Art. VIII Sec. 4 prescribes a Supreme Court composed of a Chief Justice and 14 Associate Justices — totalling 15 members.

tip.label: Mnemonic
tip.text: Supreme Court = 1 Chief + 14 Associates = 15 total. Think '1+14=15.' En banc quorum = 8. All constitutional questions require majority of the 15 who participated.

subject: General Information
question: Under the 1987 Constitution, what is the minimum age requirement to run for President of the Philippines?

choices.text: At least 35 years of age on the day of the election
At least 45 years of age on the day of the election
At least 30 years of age on the day of the election
At least 40 years of age on the day of the election
At least 40 years of age at the time of taking the oath of office

explanation: Article VII, Section 2 of the 1987 Constitution sets out the qualifications for the presidency: the candidate must be a natural-born citizen, a registered voter, able to read and write, at least forty years of age on the day of the election, and a resident of the Philippines for at least ten years immediately before the election. The 40-year minimum ensures that the occupant of the highest office has had enough life experience to lead the nation. Note that the age is reckoned on election day itself — a candidate who turns 40 on or before election day qualifies, even if they were still 39 when they filed their certificate of candidacy.

distractorExplanations.A: 35 years of age is the minimum age for a Senator (Art. VI, Sec. 3) and for Civil Service Commission members. The presidency demands a higher maturity threshold of 40.
distractorExplanations.B: 45 years of age is not prescribed by the Constitution for the presidency or any other specific office. It is a plausible distractor but has no constitutional basis.
distractorExplanations.C: 30 years of age is the minimum for a member of the House of Representatives under Article VI, Section 6. The President must be older — at least 40.
distractorExplanations.E: The age qualification is measured as of the day of the election, not the inauguration; Art. VII Sec. 2 specifies 'at least forty years of age on the day of the election'.

tip.label: Mnemonic
tip.text: Age Ladder: House member = 25, Senator = 35, President = 40. Each office steps up by 10 years. Remember: P-40, S-35, H-25.

subject: General Information
question: Article II, Section 16 of the 1987 Constitution guarantees the right of the people to what kind of ecology?

choices.text: Pristine and undisturbed ecology free from human intervention
A productive and industrialized ecology for national development
A protected ecology managed solely by the State
A sustainably developed ecology managed jointly by national and local governments.
A balanced and healthful ecology in accord with the rhythm and harmony of nature

explanation: Article II, Section 16 declares: 'The State shall protect and advance the right of the people to a balanced and healthful ecology in accord with the rhythm and harmony of nature.' Every word carries weight: 'balanced' acknowledges that environment and development must coexist; 'healthful' means the ecology must sustain human life and well-being; 'rhythm and harmony of nature' signals that human activities must not violate the ecological clock. The Supreme Court, in the landmark Oposa v. Factoran (G.R. No. 101083, 1993), held that this provision creates a self-executing right that even future generations can invoke — a concept called intergenerational responsibility.

distractorExplanations.A: The Constitution does not promise a pristine ecology untouched by humans. It calls for a 'balanced' ecology, meaning sustainable use of resources is permitted — the goal is harmony, not no-touch preservation.
distractorExplanations.B: An 'industrialized ecology' is an oxymoron and does not appear in the Constitution. The provision is explicitly protective, not developmental in the industrial sense.
distractorExplanations.C: The right belongs to the people, not just to the State. The State is the duty-bearer obligated to protect and advance this right — the people are the right-holders, not mere passive beneficiaries of state management.
distractorExplanations.D: Joint management by national and local governments is a governance mechanism, not the constitutional right described in Art. II Sec. 16; the provision guarantees individuals the right to a balanced and healthful ecology in accord with the rhythm of nature.

tip.label: Constitution Reminder
tip.text: Art. II, Sec. 16: Right to a BALANCED and HEALTHFUL ecology in accord with the RHYTHM and HARMONY of nature. Source of the Oposa doctrine on intergenerational responsibility.

subject: General Information
question: Under the 1987 Constitution, the Bill of Rights (Article III, Section 1) provides that no person shall be deprived of life, liberty, or property without which of the following?

choices.text: Approval by the Supreme Court
An act of Congress
An executive order
Due process of law
A resolution by the legislative body of the LGU concerned

explanation: Article III, Section 1 of the 1987 Constitution states: 'No person shall be deprived of life, liberty, or property without due process of law, nor shall any person be denied the equal protection of the laws.' Due process is the Constitution's great equalizer — it means the government must follow fair, lawful procedures before it can take away something so fundamental as a person's life, freedom, or property. Philippine jurisprudence recognizes two dimensions: procedural due process (proper notice and hearing) and substantive due process (the law itself must be fair and not arbitrary). Together with equal protection, this provision forms the bedrock of the entire Bill of Rights.

distractorExplanations.A: Supreme Court approval is not a constitutional prerequisite for depriving a person of life, liberty, or property. Courts may review government action, but the Constitution's requirement is adherence to 'due process of law,' a broader standard.
distractorExplanations.B: An act of Congress alone is insufficient if that act violates due process. The Constitution requires that laws themselves be substantively fair — Congress cannot simply legislate away fundamental rights.
distractorExplanations.C: An executive order alone cannot authorize deprivation of life, liberty, or property if it violates due process. Executive actions are subject to both congressional authorization and constitutional limitations.
distractorExplanations.E: An LGU legislative resolution is a local ordinance — not 'due process of law' in the constitutional sense; Art. III Sec. 1 requires due process, which encompasses procedural and substantive safeguards well beyond a simple local resolution.

tip.label: Constitution Reminder
tip.text: Art. III, Sec. 1: No deprivation of LIFE, LIBERTY, or PROPERTY without DUE PROCESS. Two types: Procedural (fair process) and Substantive (fair law). Paired with EQUAL PROTECTION in the same section.

subject: General Information
question: Under the 1987 Constitution, which among the following is a ground for impeachment of the President, Vice-President, and Members of the Supreme Court?

choices.text: Inefficiency and incompetence in the performance of official duties
Gross discourtesy to subordinates
Failure to file the Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth
Gross negligence in the performance of official duties
Betrayal of public trust

explanation: Article XI, Section 2 enumerates exactly six grounds for impeachment: culpable violation of the Constitution, treason, bribery, graft and corruption, other high crimes, and betrayal of public trust. The phrase 'betrayal of public trust' is deliberately open-ended — the framers included it as a catch-all for conduct so egregiously contrary to the people's confidence that it warrants removal, even if it does not fit a specific criminal definition. Inefficiency, discourtesy, and failure to file a SALN are administrative offenses handled through the Civil Service Commission or the Ombudsman — they do not rise to the level of constitutional grounds for removal through impeachment.

distractorExplanations.A: Inefficiency and incompetence are grounds for administrative disciplinary action under the Civil Service rules (e.g., dismissal from service), but they are not constitutional grounds for impeachment under Article XI, Section 2.
distractorExplanations.B: Gross discourtesy is a light administrative offense punishable by reprimand or suspension under CSC rules. It is nowhere near the gravity of the six enumerated impeachment grounds.
distractorExplanations.C: Failure to file a SALN is a violation of RA 6713 and may result in administrative and criminal liability, but it is not listed as an impeachment ground. SALN violations are pursued through regular legal channels, not impeachment.
distractorExplanations.D: Gross negligence is grounds for administrative disciplinary action but is NOT specifically listed as an impeachable offense; Art. XI Sec. 2 lists: culpable violation of the Constitution, treason, bribery, graft and corruption, other high crimes, and betrayal of public trust.

tip.label: Mnemonic
tip.text: Impeachment grounds: C-T-B-G-H-B. Culpable violation of the Constitution, Treason, Bribery, Graft and corruption, other High crimes, Betrayal of public trust. Six grounds only — memorize them.

subject: General Information
question: The 1987 Philippine Constitution declares in Article II, Section 7 that in its relations with other states, the paramount consideration of Philippine foreign policy shall be which of the following?

choices.text: Economic growth and foreign investment attraction
National sovereignty, territorial integrity, national interest, and the right to self-determination
Military alliances and collective defense
Adherence to international organizations and treaties
Reciprocity, mutual benefit, and alignment with ASEAN consensus positions.

explanation: Article II, Section 7 declares: 'The State shall pursue an independent foreign policy. In its relations with other states, the paramount consideration shall be national sovereignty, territorial integrity, national interest, and the right to self-determination.' These four pillars — sovereignty, territory, national interest, and self-determination — are not just aspirational; they are constitutional mandates that bind every administration's foreign policy decisions. The word 'paramount' means these considerations outrank all others, including economic benefit or alliance loyalty. This provision is why the Philippines regularly asserts its position in the West Philippine Sea disputes and reserves the right to review, renegotiate, or abrogate treaties perceived to compromise sovereignty.

distractorExplanations.A: Economic growth and investment attraction are desirable policy goals but are not what Article II, Section 7 identifies as the 'paramount consideration' of foreign policy. Economic diplomacy flows from, but is subordinate to, the four constitutional pillars.
distractorExplanations.C: Military alliances (such as the Mutual Defense Treaty with the United States) are an instrument of foreign policy, not the paramount constitutional consideration. The Constitution's emphasis on 'independent foreign policy' signals that alliances must not compromise sovereignty.
distractorExplanations.D: Adherence to international organizations and treaties is part of the Philippines' international commitments, but it is not the paramount consideration. The Constitution ranks national sovereignty and self-determination above any specific multilateral obligation.
distractorExplanations.E: While ASEAN participation and reciprocity inform Philippine diplomacy in practice, Art. II Sec. 7 grounds foreign policy on national sovereignty, territorial integrity, national interest, and the right to self-determination — not on reciprocity or ASEAN consensus as constitutional principles.

tip.label: Constitution Reminder
tip.text: Art. II, Sec. 7 = Independent foreign policy. Paramount consideration = NATIONAL SOVEREIGNTY + TERRITORIAL INTEGRITY + NATIONAL INTEREST + RIGHT TO SELF-DETERMINATION. Four pillars, one provision.

subject: General Information
question: Under the 1987 Philippine Constitution, public office is a:

choices.text: private privilege
hereditary right
commercial franchise
personal achievement
public trust

explanation: Article XI, Section 1 opens the article on accountability with one sentence and one command: 'Public office is a public trust. Public officers and employees must, at all times, be accountable to the people, serve them with utmost responsibility, integrity, loyalty, and efficiency, act with patriotism and justice, and lead modest lives.' Calling office a trust has teeth. Authority is held on behalf of the people rather than owned, so it can be withdrawn and must always be answered for. That single word is the doctrinal root of impeachment (Art. XI, Secs. 2–3), of the SALN requirement, and of the entire Code of Conduct in RA 6713.

distractorExplanations.A: A privilege is personal and exercised at the holder's pleasure — the exact opposite of a trust held for someone else. Public office confers no private entitlement to its powers or perquisites.
distractorExplanations.B: Hereditary succession describes a monarchy. Art. XI, Sec. 1 works with the republican principle of Art. II, Sec. 1: office is filled by election or merit-based appointment, never inherited.
distractorExplanations.C: A franchise is a state grant to operate a business for profit, typically a utility under Art. XII. Public office is not run for gain, which is why RA 6713 bars using one's position for private advantage.
distractorExplanations.D: Treating public office as a personal achievement or reward contradicts Art. XI Sec. 1, which declares that 'public office is a public trust' — imposing duties of accountability and full disclosure on public officials.

tip.label: Constitution Reminder
tip.text: Art. XI, Sec. 1 = 'Public office is a public trust.' Memorise the four service words — responsibility, integrity, loyalty, efficiency — then patriotism, justice, and modest lives.

subject: General Information
question: Which constitutional right protects a person from being compelled to testify against himself or herself?

choices.text: Right to travel
Right to information
Freedom of assembly
Right to bail
Right against self-incrimination

explanation: Article III, Section 17 is among the shortest provisions in the Bill of Rights: 'No person shall be compelled to be a witness against himself.' Its reach is narrower than most examinees assume. It bars compelled testimonial evidence — being forced to speak or answer in a way that helps establish one's own guilt. An accused may refuse to take the stand at all; an ordinary witness must testify but may invoke the privilege question by question as incriminating questions arise. What the clause does not do is stop the State from prosecuting, and it does not shield purely physical evidence such as fingerprints, photographs, or DNA samples.

distractorExplanations.A: Liberty of abode and the right to travel (Art. III, Sec. 6) may be impaired only in the interest of national security, public safety, or public health as provided by law. It governs movement, not testimony.
distractorExplanations.B: The right to information (Art. III, Sec. 7) lets a citizen demand records FROM the government. Sec. 17 runs the opposite way — it stops the State from extracting information out of you.
distractorExplanations.C: Art. III, Sec. 4 protects the peaceable assembly and petition of a group, a collective political right. Self-incrimination is invoked by one individual inside an investigation, hearing, or trial.
distractorExplanations.D: The right to bail (Art. III Sec. 13) is separate from the right against self-incrimination (Sec. 17); the privilege to remain silent and not be compelled to testify against oneself is specifically the right against self-incrimination.

tip.label: Exam Tip
tip.text: Self-incrimination covers COMPELLED TESTIMONY only. Accused = may refuse the witness stand entirely. Ordinary witness = must appear, then objects question by question.

subject: General Information
question: A search warrant may generally be issued only upon probable cause determined personally by:

choices.text: a police investigator
a prosecutor alone
any elected official
A court clerk acting under the judge's standing order
a judge

explanation: Article III, Section 2 allows no search warrant or warrant of arrest to issue 'except upon probable cause to be determined personally by the judge after examination under oath or affirmation of the complainant and the witnesses he may produce, and particularly describing the place to be searched and the persons or things to be seized.' The load-bearing word is 'personally': the judge must examine the applicant himself and may not delegate it or rubber-stamp a submitted affidavit. Lodging the finding with a neutral magistrate instead of the party doing the investigating is what makes the safeguard real — and evidence seized under an invalid warrant is inadmissible under the exclusionary rule of Sec. 3(2).

distractorExplanations.A: The police apply for the warrant and supply the supporting affidavits, so they are the interested party. Letting the investigator make the finding would dissolve the very check the provision was written to create.
distractorExplanations.B: Prosecutors do determine probable cause — but to FILE an information after preliminary investigation. Probable cause to ISSUE a warrant is a distinct judicial function reserved to the judge.
distractorExplanations.C: No elected executive — mayor, governor, or President — may issue a warrant. The Constitution confines the power to judges precisely because they stand outside the political and investigative process.
distractorExplanations.D: A court clerk has no authority to issue warrants; Art. III Sec. 2 requires that search warrants and warrants of arrest be personally determined and issued by a judge upon finding probable cause.

tip.label: Constitution Reminder
tip.text: Art. III, Sec. 2 four-part test: (1) probable cause, (2) determined PERSONALLY by a judge, (3) after examination under oath, (4) particular description of place and things. Fail one and Sec. 3(2) excludes the evidence.

subject: General Information
question: Which branch of government interprets laws in actual controversies?

choices.text: Executive
Legislative
Commission on Audit
Ombudsman
Judiciary

explanation: Article VIII, Section 1 vests judicial power in the Supreme Court and in such lower courts as may be established by law, and defines that power as including 'the duty of the courts of justice to settle actual controversies involving rights which are legally demandable and enforceable, and to determine whether or not there has been a grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction on the part of any branch or instrumentality of the Government.' Two phrases repay memorising. 'Actual controversies' means courts resolve live disputes between real parties — no advisory opinions on hypothetical facts. The 'grave abuse' clause is the 1987 innovation that made expanded judicial review a duty.

distractorExplanations.A: The Executive enforces and implements laws (Art. VII). Agencies necessarily read statutes to apply them, which is what makes this tempting — but their construction always yields to the courts' final interpretation.
distractorExplanations.B: Congress enacts, amends, and repeals laws (Art. VI) and can pass a clarifying statute for the future. It cannot supply the authoritative meaning of a law in a case already before the courts.
distractorExplanations.C: COA is a constitutional commission under Art. IX-D that audits government revenues and expenditures — not a branch of government at all. Its rulings are themselves reviewable by the Supreme Court.
distractorExplanations.D: The Ombudsman investigates and prosecutes public officials for graft; it does not exercise judicial review — the power to interpret laws and strike down unconstitutional acts belongs to the Judiciary (Art. VIII).

tip.label: Remember
tip.text: Legislative MAKES, Executive ENFORCES, Judiciary INTERPRETS. The constitutional commissions (CSC, COMELEC, COA), the CHR, and the Ombudsman are independent bodies — never a fourth branch.

subject: General Information
question: Under RA 6713, providing service without unfair discrimination regardless of party affiliation reflects:

choices.text: simple living
nationalism and patriotism
professionalism
political neutrality
Transparency

explanation: Section 4(A)(d) of RA 6713 states the norm of Political Neutrality: public officials and employees 'shall provide service to everyone without unfair discrimination and regardless of party affiliation or preference.' The clean test that separates this norm from its neighbours is the question each one answers. Political neutrality governs WHOM you serve equally; professionalism, at Sec. 4(A)(b), governs HOW competently you serve. A clerk who releases permits quickly but only for supporters of the winning candidate has met the standard of professionalism and breached political neutrality. This norm is also what allows a career civil service to survive a change of administration intact.

distractorExplanations.A: Simple living (Sec. 4(A)(h)) requires officials to lead modest lives appropriate to their position and income and to avoid ostentatious display of wealth. It regulates lifestyle, not client treatment.
distractorExplanations.B: Nationalism and patriotism (Sec. 4(A)(f)) demands loyalty to the Republic and promotion of Filipino products, resources, and technology. It concerns national loyalty, not partisan even-handedness.
distractorExplanations.C: Professionalism (Sec. 4(A)(b)) requires the highest degree of excellence and devotion to duty. It tempts because impartiality feels professional — but the norm named for party-blind service is political neutrality.
distractorExplanations.E: Transparency is a governance value but is not one of the eight specific norms of conduct enumerated in Sec. 4 of RA 6713; political neutrality (Sec. 4(e)) is the norm that requires public officials to be non-partisan.

tip.label: Law Reminder
tip.text: Sort the norms by the question they answer: political neutrality = WHOM you serve (everyone, regardless of party); professionalism = HOW WELL you serve; simple living = HOW you live.

subject: General Information
question: Under RA 6713, using government resources efficiently and economically primarily reflects:

choices.text: commitment to public interest
responsiveness to the public
justness and sincerity
simple living
Integrity

explanation: Section 4(A)(a) of RA 6713 defines Commitment to Public Interest: officials 'shall always uphold the public interest over and above personal interest,' and all government resources and powers 'must be employed and used efficiently, effectively, honestly and economically, particularly to avoid wastage in public funds and revenues.' Budgets, supplies, service vehicles, equipment, and paid working hours all sit inside that sentence. The line to draw is against option D: simple living governs an official's PERSONAL lifestyle and spending, while this norm governs the stewardship of PUBLIC resources. Overtime claimed for idle work and an office vehicle used for private errands are Sec. 4(A)(a) violations.

distractorExplanations.B: Responsiveness to the public (Sec. 4(A)(e)) requires extending prompt, courteous, and adequate service and providing information on policies truthfully. It is client-facing, not resource-facing.
distractorExplanations.C: Justness and sincerity (Sec. 4(A)(c)) requires acting with justice, refraining from oppressive or dishonest conduct, and giving priority to the underprivileged. It targets fairness in dealings, not thrift.
distractorExplanations.D: The classic trap, because both norms sound frugal. Simple living restrains what the official spends on himself; economical handling of government money and property is commitment to public interest.
distractorExplanations.E: Integrity is indeed a norm of conduct under Sec. 4(h) of RA 6713, but it is not the norm that requires devoting the best time and effort to public service above personal interests — that is commitment to public interest (Sec. 4(a)).

tip.label: Exam Tip
tip.text: Ask whose wallet is open. Wasting PUBLIC funds breaches commitment to public interest; flaunting PRIVATE wealth breaches simple living. Same instinct for restraint, two different wallets.

subject: General Information
question: Which is one of the norms of conduct expressly listed in RA 6713?

choices.text: Personal enrichment
Professionalism
Partisan loyalty
Preferential treatment
Compliance

explanation: RA 6713, Sec. 4(A) enumerates eight norms in this statutory order: (a) commitment to public interest, (b) professionalism, (c) justness and sincerity, (d) political neutrality, (e) responsiveness to the public, (f) nationalism and patriotism, (g) commitment to democracy, and (h) simple living. Professionalism, at letter (b), obliges officials to perform and discharge their duties 'with the highest degree of excellence, professionalism, intelligence and skill,' with utmost devotion to duty, and to discourage wrong perceptions of their roles as dispensers of undue patronage. Notice how the item is engineered: the three wrong options are not merely absent from the list — each is the precise inversion of a norm on it.

distractorExplanations.A: This inverts norm (a), commitment to public interest, which requires upholding public interest over personal interest. Enriching oneself through office is penalised by RA 3019 and RA 7080, not prescribed.
distractorExplanations.C: This inverts norm (d), political neutrality, which commands service to everyone regardless of party affiliation or preference. A public servant's loyalty runs to the Republic and the people, not a party.
distractorExplanations.D: This inverts norm (c), justness and sincerity, and is the same evil professionalism warns against when it tells officials not to act as dispensers of undue patronage.
distractorExplanations.E: Compliance with rules is expected of all officials but 'compliance' is not one of the eight norms enumerated in Sec. 4 of RA 6713; the norm requiring high standards of excellence, intelligence, and skills in public service is professionalism.

tip.label: Mnemonic
tip.text: Eight norms in statutory order — Public interest, Professionalism, Justness, Political neutrality, Responsiveness, Nationalism, Democracy, Simple living: PPJP + RNDS. If an option names a vice, it is not a norm.

subject: General Information
question: The Katipunan was founded primarily to seek:

choices.text: annexation to the United States
restoration of the galleon trade
membership in the Spanish parliament only
Autonomy within the Spanish empire through a federal arrangement
independence from Spanish rule

explanation: Andrés Bonifacio founded the Kataas-taasang, Kagalang-galangang Katipunan ng mga Anak ng Bayan in July 1892, within days of José Rizal's arrest and the order deporting him to Dapitan. That timing is the substance of the answer, not a detail: Rizal's detention convinced Bonifacio that petitioning Spain for reform had reached a dead end, so the Katipunan was organised as a secret revolutionary society aiming at separation from Spain by armed struggle. Its oath-taking rites, its Kartilya, and its cell structure all presumed a break with the colonial order rather than a better place inside it.

distractorExplanations.A: American annexation entered Philippine politics only after 1898, through the Treaty of Paris and later the Federalista party. In 1892 the United States figured nowhere in the Katipunan's programme.
distractorExplanations.B: The Manila–Acapulco galleon trade ended in 1815, three generations earlier. It was a Spanish commercial monopoly that enriched colonial officials — never a nationalist demand.
distractorExplanations.C: This is precisely what the Propaganda Movement and La Liga Filipina wanted: representation and reform WITHIN Spain. Bonifacio founded the Katipunan because that assimilationist path had failed.
distractorExplanations.D: Seeking autonomy within Spain was the goal of the reformist Propaganda Movement, not the Katipunan; the Katipunan's founding aim was complete independence from Spanish colonial rule, not a federal arrangement within Spain.

tip.label: Historical Note
tip.text: Reform versus revolution: Propaganda Movement and La Liga Filipina sought Filipino representation inside Spain; the Katipunan (1892) sought out of it. Rizal's arrest is the hinge between the two.

reference: Philippine History: Kataas-taasang, Kagalang-galangang Katipunan ng mga Anak ng Bayan (founded 1892)

subject: General Information
question: Which document proclaimed Philippine independence on June 12, 1898?

choices.text: Treaty of Paris
Malolos Constitution
Pact of Biak-na-Bato
Act of the Proclamation of Independence of the Filipino People
The Tejeros Convention Declaration

explanation: The Act of the Proclamation of Independence of the Filipino People was drafted and read aloud by Ambrosio Rianzares Bautista, Emilio Aguinaldo's war counsellor and special delegate, at Aguinaldo's house in Kawit, Cavite on 12 June 1898. The flag sewn in Hong Kong by Marcela Agoncillo was unfurled that afternoon and the Marcha Nacional Filipina was played for the first time. Dating each distractor leaves you with the entire revolutionary timeline: Pact of Biak-na-Bato in December 1897, the Act of Proclamation in June 1898, the Treaty of Paris in December 1898, and the Malolos Constitution in January 1899.

distractorExplanations.A: Signed 10 December 1898, six months AFTER the proclamation, it transferred the Philippines from Spain to the United States for $20 million. It disposed of the islands rather than freeing them.
distractorExplanations.B: Promulgated 21 January 1899, it organised the First Philippine Republic and its government. It presupposed the independence already proclaimed at Kawit; it did not proclaim it.
distractorExplanations.C: The December 1897 agreement that suspended hostilities and sent Aguinaldo into exile in Hong Kong with an indemnity. A truce with Spain is the opposite of a declaration of independence.
distractorExplanations.E: The Tejeros Convention (March 1897) reorganised the revolutionary government and transferred leadership from Bonifacio to Aguinaldo; it did not proclaim Philippine independence. The document proclaiming independence on June 12, 1898 is the Act of the Proclamation of the Independence of the Filipino People.

tip.label: Historical Note
tip.text: Sequence worth memorising: Biak-na-Bato Dec 1897 → Kawit proclamation 12 June 1898 → Treaty of Paris Dec 1898 → Malolos Constitution Jan 1899. Only the second one declares independence.

reference: Philippine History: Act of the Proclamation of Independence of the Filipino People, 12 June 1898, Kawit, Cavite

subject: General Information
question: Which law is known as the Philippine Clean Air Act of 1999?

choices.text: Republic Act No. 9003
Republic Act No. 9275
Republic Act No. 10121
Republic Act No. 8749
Republic Act No. 8550

explanation: Republic Act No. 8749 is the Philippine Clean Air Act of 1999. It builds a comprehensive air-quality management policy: airsheds as the geographic unit of regulation, national ambient air quality guideline values and emission standards, motor-vehicle emission testing as a condition of registration, and the well-known ban on incineration of municipal, biomedical, and hazardous waste. Statute-number items reward learning the family rather than the single law, because the distractors are always drawn from its siblings — air is 8749, solid waste is 9003, water is 9275, and disaster risk reduction is 10121.

distractorExplanations.A: RA 9003 is the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000 — segregation at source, materials recovery facilities, and the prohibition on new open dumps. It governs waste, not air.
distractorExplanations.B: RA 9275 is the Philippine Clean Water Act of 2004, which manages water quality through water quality management areas. Being the water twin of the Clean Air Act is exactly what makes it confusable.
distractorExplanations.C: RA 10121 is the Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010, which created the NDRRMC and its councils. Environmental in theme, but it regulates preparedness, not emissions.
distractorExplanations.E: RA 8550 is the Philippine Fisheries Code of 1998; the Clean Air Act of 1999 is Republic Act No. 8749.

tip.label: Mnemonic
tip.text: Environmental statute numbers: AIR 8749 (1999), WASTE 9003 (2000), WATER 9275 (2004), DISASTER 10121 (2010). They rise in chronological order, so the smallest number is the oldest law.

subject: General Information
question: Which practice best follows the ecological solid-waste hierarchy?

choices.text: Burn mixed waste in open areas.
Rely on landfills as the first option.
Reduce waste before considering reuse, recycling, or disposal.
Mix hazardous and biodegradable waste.
Segregate waste at source, then send all segregated materials directly to a composting facility.

explanation: RA 9003, the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000, is organised around a hierarchy: reduce → reuse → recycle → treat → dispose, with final disposal as the last resort. Section 2(c) declares the State policy of setting 'guidelines and targets for solid waste avoidance and volume reduction through source reduction and waste minimization measures, including composting, recycling, re-use, recovery, green charcoal process, and others, before collection, treatment and disposal,' while Sec. 2(d) requires best environmental practices 'excluding incineration.' Waste never generated costs nothing to collect, treat, or bury — which is why reduction at source outranks every downstream step.

distractorExplanations.A: Open burning of solid waste is a prohibited act under RA 9003, and RA 8749, Sec. 20 separately bans incineration of municipal, biomedical, and hazardous waste. Burning mixed waste also releases dioxins and furans.
distractorExplanations.B: Sanitary landfills are legitimate facilities — but they sit at the END of the hierarchy. Treating disposal as the first option inverts the statute and guarantees the very waste volumes the law exists to shrink.
distractorExplanations.D: RA 9003 mandates segregation at source. Mixing hazardous with biodegradable waste contaminates compost and recyclables and pushes toxic material into ordinary collection routes.
distractorExplanations.E: Source segregation is correct but routing everything to composting ignores the waste hierarchy; RA 9003 prescribes: reduce first, then reuse, then recycle — composting is one form of recycling, not the universal end-point for all segregated materials.

tip.label: Law Reminder
tip.text: Hierarchy order: REDUCE → REUSE → RECYCLE → TREAT → DISPOSE. Disposal is never the first answer, and burning is never an answer at all under RA 9003 and RA 8749.

reference: RA 9003 (Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000), Sec. 2

subject: General Information
question: Which gas is most abundant in Earth's atmosphere?

choices.text: Nitrogen
Oxygen
Carbon dioxide
Argon
Helium

explanation: By volume, dry air is roughly 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0.93% argon, and about 0.04% carbon dioxide, with neon, helium, and methane in trace amounts; water vapour varies from near zero to a few percent and is excluded from the 'dry air' figures. Because nitrogen and oxygen together account for about 99% of the atmosphere, every pollutant regulated under RA 8749 — particulate matter, sulfur dioxide, nitrogen dioxide, carbon monoxide, ozone, lead — is a trace constituent measured in micrograms per cubic metre or parts per million. That is exactly why small concentration changes matter so much, and why 'most abundant' and 'most consequential' are different questions.

distractorExplanations.B: Oxygen ranks second at about 21%. It sustains respiration and combustion, so it feels like it should top the list, but there is roughly four times as much nitrogen in the same volume of air.
distractorExplanations.C: Carbon dioxide is only about 0.04% of dry air. Its prominence in climate discussion makes it feel abundant — a reminder that climatic influence and sheer quantity are separate measures.
distractorExplanations.D: Argon is third at about 0.93%, the most abundant noble gas in air and used in incandescent bulbs and welding shields. Still well under 1% of the total.
distractorExplanations.E: Helium is only a trace gas in Earth's atmosphere (about 5 ppm); the most abundant atmospheric gas by volume is nitrogen at approximately 78%.

tip.label: Remember
tip.text: Dry air by volume: N₂ 78%, O₂ 21%, Ar 0.93%, CO₂ 0.04%. Nitrogen plus oxygen ≈ 99%, so every air pollutant regulated under RA 8749 is a trace gas.

reference: Atmospheric composition: dry air is approximately 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0.93% argon, and 0.04% carbon dioxide
